title: [RSS Club] Changes to the RSS and Atom feeds
content:
This content is exclusive to RSS and Atom subscribers. It is not on the web. Shhhhh!

A few weeks ago I accidentally broke some of your feed readers. I was using <![CDATA[ … ]]> blocks in the feed. That allows me to put in raw HTML without the need for escaping. Unfortunately, some feed readers unescaped text which should have remained escaped. Confusing, innit?

Anyway, if you've a mind to, I'd be grateful if you let me know if this post does anything "weird" with your reader0.

This text should be bold but this text <strong>should not</strong>.

This text should be escaped <marquee> and should not cause your reader to scroll.

This is an image of a mushroom cloud:

This is the escaped version <img src="https://shkspr.mobi/blog/wp-content/uploads/2012/08/atomic-bomb-2621291_640.jpg" alt="A glowing red mushroom cloud caused by an atomic bomb." width="640" height="427" class="aligncenter" />

This should just be an ampersand:

&

And this should be ampersand, amp, and semicolon:

&

Here's a video embed that I like:

I'm sure there's all sorts of other odd stuff I could add, but this'll be a good start.

With thanks to Suren Enfiajyan's article for the guidance.

  1. I mean weirder than my usual stuff! ↩︎

title: “I’m Embarrassed on Behalf of the Tech Industry”
content:
That’s something Ben Thompson said a recent episode of Dithering. He was referring to how he felt while trying to help his mom get control of her digital life. Everything was just too hard and convoluted and he felt embarrassed as someone who works in tech.

That very same evening, I randomly got this text from a family member.

I hear this a lot from family and friends who sit outside tech.

“Nothing works.”

“Everything is hard to use.”

“I can’t make sense of this.”

And to them I am a representative, a connection, to this pain in their lives.

And I, too, am embarrassed on behalf of the tech industry — by our collective failure.

title: How fast is Python 3.15?
content:
It's October once again, and that means it is time to take the new release of Python for a spin. As I did with my Python 3.14 performance article of a year ago, today I'm sharing a new run of my informal Python benchmark, comparing Python 3.15 against previous interpreters all the way back to 3.10.

If you are not interested in the charts and the tables and just want to read my analysis, feel free to jump to the conclusions section at the end.
